name: Renaissance
lede: Renaissance is a deep raspberry crimson, a shade name from an early twentieth-century color dictionary; it is not the name of any documented dye or painter's pigment of the period it recalls.

sections.title: A dictionary shade
sections.body:
The name comes from Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930), which places Renaissance on plate 52, square L 9, and dates its first record to 1924 [1]. The dictionary files it under fashion and textiles [1]. Who coined it, and what it was first used on, is undocumented in the sources we checked [1][2].

The swatch is dark and strongly colored, lightness 35 and chroma 45, and its nearest named neighbor in our library is [[raspberry]], six units away [1]. By eye it sits in the family of [[crimson]] and [[burgundy]] [1].

sections.title: What Renaissance Europe wore
sections.body:
Greenfield describes a world in which grey and beige were the colors of poverty, worn by the poorest people and by lowly priests, monks and nuns [3]. Red was the opposite: kermes dye cost nearly twice as much as green at one Florentine dyeshop, and at another it cost ten times as much to dye cloth [[scarlet]] as to dye it sky blue [3]. Scarlet caps and turbans were a fashion for upwardly mobile men, and Jan van Eyck painted a man in one [3].

What exactly scarlet and crimson meant in this period is, by Greenfield's account, a matter of debate [3]. A rich household could be hung with crimson as well: Sir William Cecil, Queen Elizabeth's secretary of state, slept in a bed hung with crimson velvet [4]. A color like this swatch is in the neighborhood of that crimson, though no source ties the dictionary name to any of these dyes [1][3][4].

sections.title: What painters had to work with
sections.body:
Ball makes the surprising point that the Renaissance painter's palette was scarcely broader than the medieval one, since mixing pigments was taboo until oil painting made it acceptable [5]. [[vermilion|Vermilion]], scarce and costly in medieval manuscripts, was ubiquitous in Renaissance painting [6]. Titian used orpiment and realgar, the only true orange of the period, which was available in Venice from around 1490 [5]. Alberti wrote his *Della Pittura* in 1435 and advised on placing light colors beside dark ones [5][7].

The period also thought about color differently. Leonardo ranked six colors, each tied to an element: white to light, yellow to earth, green to water, blue to air, red to fire and black to darkness [8][9]. Pastoureau notes that six basic colors, not three, were the rule in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, and that blue was then often counted a warm color [10][11]. The long argument over *disegno* against *colore*, drawing against color, ran through the Renaissance and treated color as the lesser art [12].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, only 8 contain this color: within six units (ΔE 2000) of #912D4C and covering at least five per cent of the canvas [13]. None of the 3,619 works made before 1600 do, and the archive's 25 paintings tagged Renaissance include none [13]. The earliest match is Jusepe de Ribera's *Saint John the Baptist in the Desert*, about 1650, at 10 per cent of the canvas [[painter:jusepe-de-ribera|Ribera]] [13].

Six of the eight come from India, which is about 3 per cent of the archive (721 works), and two of those are Mughal [13]. The largest field is in Paul Sérusier's *Les trois fileuses* of 1915, at 25 per cent [[painting:commons-Q17493804|Les trois fileuses]] [13]. So the color named for the Renaissance is, in our data, a color of the 1900s and of India [13].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a color match and not a pigment test [13].
